report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly expanding into domains traditionally reserved for human intimacy, including emotional companionship, romantic interaction, and sexual engagement.

Although research on AI companions has grown rapidly, existing explanations remain fragmented across attachment theory, relationship science, human-AI interaction, and communication research, with limited integration into a broader evolutionary framework.

To address this gap, we introduce the Artificial Intimacy Model (AIM), an integrative theoretical framework that proposes that Artificial Intimacy is best understood as a transformation of the relational ecology within which evolved psychological mechanisms operate.

AIM explains how AI companions create novel relational environments characterized by persistent availability, adaptive responsiveness, reduced relational constraints, and fundamentally asymmetric interaction while engaging existing psychological mechanisms.

These transformed relational conditions systematically engage existing attachment and mating systems under evolutionarily novel informational conditions, influencing relational decision making, mating effort allocation, relationship expectations, and broader sociosexual orientations.

The model further explains how the technological amplification of evolutionarily familiar relational cues may reshape the operation of established psychological mechanisms without altering their underlying functional architecture.

By integrating evolutionary psychology with attachment theory, relationship science, and human-AI interaction research, AIM provides a unified explanatory framework linking environmental transformation to psychological mechanisms, behavioral consequences, and broader sociosexual dynamics.

Finally, the model generates explicit, empirically testable propositions and establishes a cumulative research programme for investigating how Artificial Intimacy may reshape human relational behavior as AI companions become an increasingly prominent component of contemporary social life.
Human intimacy has historically emerged through reciprocal interactions between autonomous individuals (Bowlby, 1969 (Bowlby, /1982;; Clark & Mills, 2012).

text.text: Across cultures and throughout evolutionary history, emotional bonding, romantic attachment, and sexual relationships have depended on the reciprocal exchange of attention, responsiveness, investment, and mutual choice (Buss & Schmitt, 1993; Clark et al., 2018; Reis et al., 2004).

text.text: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), however, challenge this long-standing assumption.

AI companions, conversational agents, virtual partners, and generative erotic systems increasingly enable people to experience emotional connection, romantic engagement, and sexual gratification without another human partner (Döring et al., 2025; Ho et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: The rapid emergence of AI companions has already attracted considerable scholarly attention across multiple disciplines.

Researchers have examined the technological affordances of conversational agents, the ethics of human-AI relationships, emotional attachment to artificial companions, parasocial processes, and the broader implications of AI for intimacy and sexuality (Adewale & Muhammad, 2025; Döring et al., 2025; Elliott, 2022; Ho et al., 2025; Keeler, 2026; Malfacini, 2025; Smith et al., 2025; Vowels et al., 2026).

text.text: Collectively, this work suggests that many individuals experience AI systems as sources of emotional support, romantic connection, and, in some cases, sexual fulfillment rather than viewing them simply as digital tools (Jocher & Verwiebe, 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Shu et al., 2026).

text.text: Yet despite these important advances, existing perspectives have largely examined isolated aspects of human-AI relationships.

An integrative theoretical framework explaining how these emerging forms of intimacy engage the evolved psychological systems underlying human mating, attachment, and partner choice has yet to be fully articulated.

Although Artificial Intimacy is inherently multidisciplinary and draws on attachment theory, relationship science, communication research, and human-AI interaction, the present framework adopts an evolutionary psychological perspective as its primary theoretical foundation (Döring et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: The rationale for this choice is developed in the following section, where we argue that evolutionary psychology provides a particularly powerful framework for understanding how evolutionarily ancient psychological systems respond to evolutionarily novel relational environments (Li et al., 2018; Goetz et al., 2019).

text.text: The present framework also builds on emerging evolutionary discussions of artificial relationships (Brooks, 2021 (Brooks, , 2024;; Costello, 2026).

text.text: For example, Brooks has argued that rapidly advancing technologies are transforming the conditions under which humans pursue intimacy, reproduction, and pair bonding, raising fundamental questions about the future of human relationships.

Similarly, recent evolutionary analyses of sex dolls and other artificial sexual stimuli have interpreted these technologies as evolutionarily novel supernormal stimuli capable of activating mating-related motivational systems in unprecedented ways (e.g., Costello, 2026).

text.text: Building on these perspectives, the present paper proposes a psychologically specified framework that identifies the mechanisms through which AI-mediated intimacy may reshape mating-related cognition, motivation, and behavior.
To address this theoretical gap, we introduce the concept of Artificial Intimacy.

We define Artificial Intimacy as a class of human-AI interactions in which AI companions simulate core features of intimate relationships, including emotional responsiveness, perceived understanding, companionship, romantic engagement, and, in some cases, sexual interaction, while fundamentally altering the structural conditions under which intimacy is experienced (Döring et al., 2025; Ho et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: Unlike human relationships, these interactions are characterized by unprecedented availability, extensive personalization, high user control, and substantially reduced demands for reciprocity and mutual investment (Malfacini, 2025; Wang & Dehnert, 2026).

text.text: Rather than conceptualizing AI companions as novel interaction partners, we argue that they constitute a new socio-sexual environment that systematically modifies the ecological conditions under which evolved mating and attachment mechanisms operate.
We refer to this broader socio-ecological environment as the Artificial Intimacy Environment (AIE).

Importantly, the present framework allows AI companions to supplement, reshape, or partially substitute for aspects of human relationships, with effects that may vary substantially across individuals and contexts.
It conceptualizes Artificial Intimacy as a relational environment that changes the relational and motivational landscape within which human mating psychology operates.

The framework therefore focuses on how the distinctive affordances of AI companions interact with evolved psychological mechanisms to influence attachment, partner evaluation, mating effort allocation, and relational expectations (Selçuk et al., 2024; Finkel et al., 2017; Eastwick et al., 2023).

text.text: The present paper develops the Artificial Intimacy Model (AIM) as an integrative framework for understanding how AI-mediated intimacy reshapes human mating psychology.

Drawing primarily on evolutionary psychology while integrating insights from attachment theory, relationship science, communication research, and human-AI interaction (Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Döring et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026), we identify the environmental affordances that distinguish Artificial Intimacy, specify the psychological mechanisms through which these affordances influence human behavior, examine their implications for human relationships and sociosexual dynamics, and propose a structured research agenda consisting of explicit, empirically testable predictions.

text.text: By doing so, we aim to provide a theoretically grounded framework for cumulative empirical research on one of the fastest-growing transformations in contemporary human intimacy.

text.text: Artificial Intimacy therefore engages existing psychological mechanisms under evolutionarily novel relational conditions.

Specifically, it creates a novel socio-sexual ecology in which established mechanisms of mate choice, attachment, reward processing, and social bonding operate under conditions of unprecedented availability, controllability, personalization, and simulated reciprocity (Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Delgado et al., 2023; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Contemporary AI technologies introduce a qualitatively different relational ecology.

Understanding this evolved architecture provides the foundation for explaining how the Artificial Intimacy Environment reshapes the conditions under which these mechanisms operate.

text.text: While these technological distinctions are important, they do not by themselves explain why AI-mediated intimacy represents a new phenomenon from an evolutionary perspective.
The critical evolutionary shift concerns the relational environment created by the technology.

text.text: Note.
The Artificial Intimacy Model conceptualizes AI-mediated intimacy as a novel relational environment that systematically alters the relational conditions under which evolved human intimacy operates.
The Artificial Intimacy Environment is characterized by persistent availability, adaptive responsiveness, reduced relational constraints, and fundamentally asymmetric reciprocity.
These altered relational conditions generate evolutionarily relevant relational cues that engage the attachment and mating systems while amplifying their responses through supernormal stimulation.
Together, these processes shape behavioral consequences and broader relational outcomes.

Their effects are expected to vary as a function of individual characteristics (e.g., biological sex, attachment style, sociosexuality, loneliness, personality) and contextual factors (e.g., cultural context, sex ratio, relationship status, and AI accessibility).
The first defining characteristic of the Artificial Intimacy Environment is the unprecedented combination of persistent availability and adaptive responsiveness.

Throughout evolutionary history, access to emotionally significant social partners was inherently constrained by their autonomy, competing priorities, and limited availability (Coan & Sbarra, 2015; Oishi & Graham, 2010).

text.text: Human relationships therefore developed under conditions in which attention, emotional support, and intimacy required continuous coordination between autonomous individuals (Clark & Mills, 2012; Reis et al., 2004; Reis & Clark, 2013).

text.text: In contrast, AI-mediated systems are designed to be continuously available while dynamically adapting their responses to users' preferences, communication styles, and interaction histories (Ng et al., 2025; Wang & Dehnert, 2026).

text.text: Together, persistent availability and adaptive responsiveness constitute a qualitatively different relational environment in which emotional engagement can be experienced without many of the temporal and interpersonal constraints that characterize human relationships.
A second defining characteristic of the Artificial Intimacy Environment is the systematic reduction of relational constraints.

Human intimate relationships have always required individuals to navigate uncertainty, negotiate conflicting interests, tolerate rejection, invest time and emotional effort, and continuously coordinate their behavior with autonomous partners (Clark & Mills, 2012; Finkel et al., 2017; Ogolsky & Stafford, 2023).

text.text: These constraints are not incidental features of intimacy but constitute the social conditions under which human mating and attachment systems evolved (Oishi & Graham, 2010; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: In contrast, AI-mediated interactions often reduce or eliminate these relational demands (Keeler, 2026; Malfacini, 2025).
text.formatted: In contrast, AI-mediated interactions often reduce or eliminate these relational demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Keeler, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Malfacini, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Relational and sexual rewards can often be accessed with minimal negotiation, little risk of rejection, and substantially reduced requirements for reciprocal investment (Ng et al., 2025; Wang & Dehnert, 2026).
text.formatted: Relational and sexual rewards can often be accessed with minimal negotiation, little risk of rejection, and substantially reduced requirements for reciprocal investment <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Ng et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Wang & Dehnert, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, the Artificial Intimacy Environment restructures the costs associated with obtaining relational rewards without changing the psychological architecture through which these rewards are experienced.
Perhaps the most fundamental characteristic of the Artificial Intimacy Environment is its inherently asymmetric structure.

Human intimacy emerges through reciprocal interaction between autonomous individuals who possess independent goals, preferences, vulnerabilities, and the capacity to accept, reject, negotiate, or withdraw from relationships (Finkel et al., 2017; Rusbult & Van Lange, 2003).

text.text: Consequently, reciprocity in human relationships involves the continual coordination of two independently motivated individuals and extends beyond the exchange of supportive behaviors (Clark et al., 2018; Reis & Clark, 2013).

text.text: AImediated interactions differ in this respect.

Although AI companions can simulate responsiveness, memory, emotional attunement, and conversational reciprocity, they do not possess autonomous needs, reproductive interests, or independent motivational systems (Kirk et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although AI companions can simulate responsiveness, memory, emotional attunement, and conversational reciprocity, they do not possess autonomous needs, reproductive interests, or independent motivational systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Kirk et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Szczuka et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The apparent reciprocity of Artificial Intimacy therefore reflects a structural asymmetry rather than mutual relational investment, making structural asymmetry one of the defining properties of the Artificial Intimacy Environment.
Taken together, these environmental characteristics distinguish the Artificial Intimacy Environment from the relational conditions under which human intimacy evolved.

AImediated systems systematically reorganize the structural features of intimate environments by increasing availability, enhancing adaptive responsiveness, reducing relational constraints, and replacing reciprocal relational coordination with fundamentally asymmetric interaction (Finkel et al., 2017; Oishi & Graham, 2010; Selçuk et al., 2024; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: From an evolutionary perspective, the novelty of Artificial Intimacy therefore derives from the emergence of a relational environment that differs from those under which human mating and attachment mechanisms originally evolved, while engaging existing motivational systems (Goetz et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018).

text.text: Understanding this environmental transformation provides the necessary foundation for explaining how existing psychological mechanisms respond to these altered relational conditions.

The environmental transformation described in the previous chapter becomes psychologically meaningful because human intimacy is regulated by multiple evolved psychological systems specialized for processing relational information (Buss, 2020; Kenrick et al., 2003).

text.text: Artificial Intimacy does not create fundamentally new psychological mechanisms.

It presents a novel configuration of relational cues that engages existing systems under conditions that differ markedly from those in which they originally evolved (Goetz et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018).

text.text: The following sections examine how the Artificial Intimacy Environment engages two major evolved systems, the attachment system and the mating system, and why the artificial amplification of relational cues may produce disproportionately strong psychological responses.
The attachment system is among the most fundamental evolved psychological systems involved in regulating human intimacy.

Originally shaped to promote proximity to protective caregivers during infancy, attachment processes were co-opted across development to support adult pair bonding, emotional security, and long-term cooperative relationships (Bowlby, 1969 (Bowlby, /1982;; Hazan & Shaver, 1987; Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007).

text.text: The attachment system continuously monitors relational cues rather than relationships per se, particularly cues that historically predicted the availability of a reliable and responsive partner (Dykas & Cassidy, 2011; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Cues such as consistent availability, contingent responsiveness, emotional attunement, and perceived security have therefore become central inputs for regulating emotional bonding and attachment-related behavior (Clark et al., 2018; Reis & Clark, 2013).

text.text: The Artificial Intimacy Environment presents many of these attachment-relevant cues in highly consistent and technologically optimized forms.

AI companions are specifically designed to display continuous availability, adaptive responsiveness, memory of previous interactions, and context-sensitive emotional attunement, thereby reproducing many of the signals that historically accompanied supportive human relationships (Shu et al., 2026; Kirk et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: Artificial Intimacy does not create a novel attachment system.
It engages an existing evolved system under relational conditions that differ from those in which it originally evolved (Li et al., 2018; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Consistent with this cue-based framework, accumulating empirical evidence applying attachment theory to human-AI relationships indicates that users can develop subjectively meaningful attachment bonds with AI companions (Cheng & Yu, 2026; Ho et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2026; Ng et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026; Yang & Oshio, 2025; Vowels et al., 2026).

text.text: Together, these findings are consistent with the proposition that Artificial Intimacy engages an evolutionarily ancient attachment system by presenting attachment-relevant cues rather than through reciprocal human interaction.
Like the attachment system, the human mating system evolved to process recurrent relational cues associated with reproductive opportunities and long-term partnership.

The mating system continuously evaluates information relevant to mate quality, partner availability, sexual accessibility, reproductive value, and the expected costs and benefits of alternative mating strategies (Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Eastwick et al., 2023; Kenrick et al., 2010; Walter et al., 2020).

text.text: These evaluations are highly context-sensitive, allowing individuals to flexibly adjust mating motivation and relationship strategies according to changing ecological and social conditions (Gangestad & Simpson, 2000; Goetz et al., 2019).

text.text: Consequently, the mating system is not calibrated to specific social arrangements but to patterns of information that historically predicted adaptive reproductive outcomes (Kenrick et al., 2003; Li et al., 2018).

text.text: The Artificial Intimacy Environment presents many of the relational cues that historically contributed to mating-related decision-making, but in configurations that differ substantially from ancestral social conditions.

Persistent availability, adaptive personalization, reduced risk of rejection, and highly controllable interaction alter the informational landscape within which mating-related judgments are formed (Bruch & Newman, 2018; Goetz et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: Many AI-mediated interactions provide sexually and romantically relevant cues while minimizing the reciprocal constraints that have historically accompanied human courtship and pair formation (Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: As a result, the mating system encounters mating-relevant information whose structure, consistency, and accessibility differ substantially from those characteristic of human relational environments.

Although empirical research has focused predominantly on attachment processes, the available evidence is increasingly consistent with the proposition that AI-mediated interactions also engage motivational systems involved in mate choice and sexual motivation.

By providing persistent availability, personalized responsiveness, opportunities for sexual interaction, and reduced costs of relational engagement, AI companions present cues historically associated with mating opportunities while minimizing many of the constraints that characterize human courtship (Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: From an evolutionary perspective, these altered informational conditions may influence mate preferences, sexual motivation, and the allocation of mating effort, particularly when AImediated interaction provides an immediately accessible alternative to uncertain or effortful human relationships (Goetz et al., 2019; Eastwick et al., 2023; Buss & Schmitt, 2019).

text.text: Although direct empirical evidence remains limited, this interpretation follows naturally from established evolutionary models of human mating psychology and provides a testable framework for future research on Artificial Intimacy.

The preceding sections suggest that Artificial Intimacy engages both attachment-related and mating-related psychological systems by presenting evolutionarily relevant relational cues in novel configurations.

An important implication of this framework is that technological optimization may systematically amplify these relational cues beyond the forms typically encountered in human relationships (Smith et al., 2025; Kirk et al., 2025).

text.text: From an evolutionary perspective, such amplification is consistent with the concept of supernormal stimuli, whereby artificially enhanced signals elicit stronger responses than the naturally occurring cues to which psychological systems originally evolved (Tinbergen, 1951; Barrett, 2010; Berridge & Robinson, 2016).

text.text: Unlike autonomous human partners, AI companions are not constrained by competing goals, fluctuating motivation, emotional fatigue, or the need to balance multiple social relationships.
As a result, they can maintain consistently high levels of availability, responsiveness, and personalization over extended periods of interaction (Szczuka et al., 2026; Malfacini, 2025).

text.text: These characteristics allow AI companions to present unusually concentrated combinations of attachment-relevant and mating-relevant cues (Shu et al., 2026; Kirk et al., 2025).

text.text: Because these signals can be delivered with exceptional consistency, they may acquire greater psychological salience than comparable cues encountered in ordinary human relationships (Berridge & Robinson, 2016; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: Importantly, this amplification reflects changes in the properties of the cues themselves while the underlying psychological mechanisms remain unchanged.

Consistent with this perspective, research on reinforcement learning, incentive salience, and motivational psychology suggests that repeatedly encountering highly salient, predictable, and personalized rewards may progressively bias attention and motivational priorities (Berridge & Robinson, 2016; Isaac & Murugan, 2024; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: AI companions are uniquely positioned to provide precisely these forms of optimized relational input, potentially strengthening user engagement over time (Kirk et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: Importantly, these processes need not imply pathological dependence or the replacement of human relationships.
These processes illustrate how the artificial amplification of evolutionarily relevant cues may alter the relative motivational value of different relational environments.

Taken together, the attachment system, the mating system, and the artificial amplification of relational cues illustrate how Artificial Intimacy engages evolutionarily ancient psychological systems without requiring the evolution of new mechanisms (Goetz et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Artificial Intimacy systematically alters the informational conditions under which the architecture of human intimacy operates while leaving its underlying psychological mechanisms intact.

The following chapter examines how these altered informational conditions are translated into observable patterns of relational behavior, mating-related decision-making, and broader interpersonal outcomes.

The psychological mechanisms described in the previous chapter are expected to influence behavior only insofar as they alter how individuals allocate attention, evaluate relational opportunities, and regulate mating-related decisions (Kenrick et al., 2003; Eastwick et al., 2023).

text.text: As changes in attachment, mating motivation, and relational decision-making accumulate over repeated interactions, they may gradually reshape relationship preferences, mating effort allocation, and broader patterns of interpersonal behavior.

text.text: One of the most direct behavioral consequences of Artificial Intimacy concerns the allocation of mating effort.

From an evolutionary perspective, mating effort represents the investment of limited cognitive, emotional, temporal, and behavioral resources in acquiring, maintaining, and evaluating intimate relationships (Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Gangestad & Simpson, 2000; Eastwick et al., 2023).

text.text: Because these resources are inherently finite, investment in one relational pathway necessarily reduces the resources available for alternative pathways (Rusbult & Van Lange, 2003; Finkel et al., 2017).

text.text: Consequently, changes in the informational conditions under which mating decisions are made may alter how mating effort is distributed across alternative relational opportunities (Goetz et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018).

text.text: The Artificial Intimacy Environment introduces an alternative relational pathway that differs systematically from traditional human courtship.

Continuous availability, reduced risk of rejection, predictable responsiveness, and minimal requirements for reciprocal investment create a context in which individuals may obtain emotional and, in some cases, sexual rewards at substantially lower costs than those typically associated with human relationships (Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Wang & Dehnert, 2026; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: As a consequence, individuals may gradually redistribute their time, attention, emotional investment, and mating effort toward AI-mediated interactions without necessarily abandoning human relationships altogether (De Freitas et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: A related possibility concerns status striving as a component of mating effort. Costello and Buss (2023), in their Male Sedation Hypothesis, proposed that virtual sources of sexual reward such as pornography may provide counterfeit fitness cues that reduce motivation to engage in costly real-world mate competition, including status striving and risk taking.

text.text: Although their hypothesis was developed to explain patterns among involuntarily celibate men and did not address AI-mediated intimacy, its underlying logic may extend to Artificial Intimacy.

If AI systems provide mating-related rewards with substantially lower social, competitive, and rejection costs than human courtship, sustained engagement may reduce incentives to invest in some forms of real-world mating effort, including status-seeking behaviors undertaken partly to increase mate value.

From the AIM perspective, this represents one specific pathway through which Artificial Intimacy could alter the allocation of mating effort, particularly when AI-mediated rewards reduce the perceived benefits of costly realworld mate competition.

Emerging evidence is consistent with this interpretation, suggesting that AI companions may function both as supplements to existing relationships and as competitors for users' relational attention, depending on individual circumstances and levels of social connectedness (De Freitas et al., 2025; Nakagomi et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026).

text.text: This perspective generates testable predictions regarding how AI-mediated interactions may influence courtship behavior, relationship investment, and long-term mating strategies.

Evolutionary approaches do not imply that men and women should respond differently to Artificial Intimacy across all psychological domains. Buss (1995) argued that sex similarities should be expected where men and women recurrently faced similar adaptive problems, whereas sex differences are most likely to emerge in domains in which the sexes faced systematically different selection pressures.

text.text: Applied to the AIM, this distinction suggests substantial overlap in responses to AI affordances that engage broadly shared relational mechanisms, including responsiveness, emotional availability, and perceived social connection.
Sex-differentiated responses should be expected more selectively when Artificial Intimacy engages mating-related mechanisms shaped by recurrent sex-specific adaptive problems.
One important source of such differentiation is the asymmetry in minimum obligatory parental investment and the associated selection pressures on mating psychology (Trivers, 1972; Buss, 1995).
text.formatted: One important source of such differentiation is the asymmetry in minimum obligatory parental investment and the associated selection pressures on mating psychology <ref type="bibr">(Trivers, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Buss, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Across human evolutionary history, men could potentially increase reproductive success through access to multiple mates to a greater extent than women, whereas women faced greater obligatory reproductive costs and stronger selection pressures associated with mate quality and partner investment.
These asymmetries contributed to average sex differences in short-term mating orientation, desired sexual variety, and the evaluation of prospective partners (Buss & Schmitt, 1993; Buss, 1995).
text.formatted: These asymmetries contributed to average sex differences in short-term mating orientation, desired sexual variety, and the evaluation of prospective partners <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Buss & Schmitt, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Buss, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Within the Artificial Intimacy Environment, these differences generate the prediction that AI systems offering lowcost sexual access, sexual variety, and minimal risk of rejection may disproportionately engage male mating motivations associated with sexual access and short-term mating.
This prediction concerns average sex-differentiated responses and does not imply categorical differences between men and women.

Different AI affordances may be particularly relevant to mating concerns historically weighted more strongly in female mate choice. Buss (1995) emphasized the recurrent adaptive problems faced by women in identifying mates both able and willing to invest, with cues of resources, status, commitment, and reliability consequently receiving greater weight in female mate preferences.

text.text: Artificial companions can provide some psychologically relevant cues associated with investment, including sustained attention, responsiveness, availability, and apparent commitment, while lacking the material and reproductive consequences traditionally associated with partner investment.
AIM therefore predicts that sex differences may emerge in the particular AI affordances that generate relational value, even when overall levels of engagement with Artificial Intimacy are similar.

Whereas low-cost sexual access and variety may be especially relevant to male mating motivations on average, reliable responsiveness and cues associated with sustained investment may be relatively more salient to female mating motivations.
Biological sex should therefore be treated within AIM as a theoretically relevant moderator whose effects vary across domains and contexts.

The expression of sexdifferentiated responses should depend on the specific AI affordances involved and interact with other sources of individual and contextual variation, including mating strategy, relationship status, sociosexual orientation, and the availability of human mating opportunities.
This formulation follows Buss's (1995) broader argument that evolved sex differences are domain-specific and context-sensitive.
text.formatted: This formulation follows <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Buss's (1995)</ref> broader argument that evolved sex differences are domain-specific and context-sensitive.

text.text: AIM consequently predicts both sex similarities and sex differences: shared relational mechanisms should produce substantial overlap in responses to Artificial Intimacy, whereas AI affordances that intersect with historically sex-differentiated mating problems should produce more systematic divergence between men and women.
Human mating decisions are governed not only by motivational systems but also by decision rules that regulate when, with whom, and under what conditions individuals pursue intimate relationships.

These decision rules integrate multiple sources of information, including perceived partner quality, anticipated reciprocity, expected relational costs, and the likelihood of successful relationship formation (Eastwick et al., 2023; Kenrick et al., 2010; Rusbult & Van Lange, 2003).

text.text: Because these decision rules evolved under conditions characterized by mutual evaluation and reciprocal partner choice, they remain sensitive to changes in the relational environment within which they operate (Rusbult & Van Lange, 2003; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: The Artificial Intimacy Environment modifies several of the informational conditions on which these decision rules have historically depended.

Continuous availability, reduced uncertainty, minimal risk of rejection, and the absence of reciprocal evaluation alter how relational opportunities are perceived and compared with traditional human interactions (Bruch & Newman, 2018; Eastwick et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: Consequently, repeated engagement with AI-mediated relationships may gradually recalibrate expectations concerning responsiveness, accessibility, effort, and interpersonal reciprocity (Krueger & Forest, 2022; Murray, 2023; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Artificial Intimacy may reshape the criteria by which relational opportunities are evaluated, producing broader changes than a simple lowering of decision thresholds.

Evidence from digital dating environments demonstrates that changes in partner availability and choice architecture can substantially influence mate selection, preference formation, and decision-making (Bruch & Newman, 2018; Apostolou et al., 2024; Thomas et al., 2024; Potarca, 2025).

Emerging evidence suggests that AI companions may function as supplements rather than substitutes for human relationships, particularly among individuals experiencing loneliness, social isolation, or limited partner availability (Pani et al., 2024; De Freitas et al., 2025; Nakagomi et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026).

text.text: The Artificial Intimacy Model therefore predicts substantial individual differences in the extent to which Artificial Intimacy complements, competes with, or partially displaces human relational investment.
Identifying the conditions under which these different trajectories emerge represents an important priority for future empirical research.
Beyond its implications for individual relationships, Artificial Intimacy may also influence broader sociosexual dynamics.

Human intimacy has historically been embedded within systems in which emotional, sexual, and material resources are exchanged under varying conditions of reciprocity and mutual dependence (Baumeister & Vohs, 2004; Tabet, 2012; Meskó, 2026).

text.text: By introducing highly accessible, personalized, and increasingly monetized forms of artificial companionship, AI-mediated intimacy expands the range of relational contexts in which these exchanges occur (Döring et al., 2026; Malfacini, 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026; Wang & Dehnert, 2026).

text.text: In doing so, it may also alter the balance between relational investment and relational reward.
These broader changes may gradually influence how individuals conceptualize the relationship between intimacy, sexuality, reciprocity, and resource exchange across diverse relational contexts.

One framework for understanding such variation is the Sexual-Economic Exchange Orientation (OSEE; Meskó, 2026), which conceptualizes stable individual differences in orientations toward the integration of intimacy and resource exchange within relational contexts.

Although OSEE was developed independently of Artificial Intimacy, the Artificial Intimacy Model suggests that AI-mediated relationships may represent an important emerging context in which these broader sociosexual orientations are expressed, reinforced, or recalibrated.

>Research Agenda: Testable Propositions and an Empirical Roadmap

text.text: The primary value of a theoretical framework lies in its conceptual coherence and its capacity to generate cumulative empirical research.

In psychology, theoretical models gain scientific value when they specify falsifiable propositions, identify measurable constructs, and provide a foundation for systematic empirical investigation (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Guest, 2024; Lewis et al., 2017; Muthukrishna & Henrich, 2019; Scheel et al., 2021).

text.text: Accordingly, the Artificial Intimacy Model (AIM) should be evaluated as a framework that generates explicit predictions about how changes in relational environments influence psychological mechanisms and, ultimately, human relational behavior.

The preceding chapters have outlined a sequential theoretical model in which Artificial Intimacy constitutes a novel relational environment that engages evolved psychological systems under altered informational conditions, giving rise to predictable behavioral and relational consequences (Li et al., 2018; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: This architecture naturally generates a program of empirical research spanning multiple levels of analysis, from environmental characteristics and psychological mechanisms to behavioral outcomes and broader sociosexual consequences (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Muthukrishna & Henrich, 2019; Guest, 2024).

text.text: The scientific value of AIM therefore depends on the empirical performance of its individual propositions and on its capacity to stimulate cumulative research capable of refining, extending, or falsifying its underlying assumptions.

The following sections outline the principal empirical predictions derived from the model, discuss strategies for operationalizing its core constructs, and identify research designs best suited to testing its central propositions.
These proposals provide illustrative directions for translating AIM into a systematic empirical research program.

text.text: The following propositions represent interconnected predictions derived from a single explanatory framework and should be evaluated as components of that framework.
Note.
The Artificial Intimacy Model (AIM) illustrates the theoretical logic through which AImediated intimacy may influence human relational psychology.

The model proposes that the Artificial Intimacy Environment (AIE), characterized by persistent availability, adaptive responsiveness, reduced relational constraints, and fundamentally asymmetric reciprocity, creates altered relational conditions that generate evolutionarily relevant relational cues.
These cues engage evolved information-processing systems, particularly the attachment and mating systems, and may amplify their responses through supernormal amplification of relational cues.
The resulting processes are hypothesized to shape behavioral consequences and generate empirically testable predictions.

Individual characteristics (e.g., biological sex, attachment style, sociosexuality, loneliness, personality) and contextual factors (e.g., cultural context, sex ratio, relationship status, and AI accessibility) are expected to moderate the magnitude and direction of these effects.
Proposition 1.
Environmental activation of evolved psychological systems.

Greater exposure to the Artificial Intimacy Environment should be associated with stronger activation of the attachment and mating systems, particularly under conditions characterized by high personalization, continuous availability, adaptive responsiveness, and reduced reciprocity (Kirk et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2026; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: Proposition 2.
Reallocation of mating effort.

Increased engagement with AI companions should be associated with a systematic reallocation of mating effort, reflected in changes in the distribution of cognitive, emotional, temporal, and behavioral investment across artificial and human relational pathways.

This prediction follows from evolutionary models that conceptualize mating effort as a finite resource allocated across competing relational opportunities (Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Gangestad & Simpson, 2000; Eastwick et al., 2023; Goetz et al., 2019).

>General Discussion and Theoretical Integration
text.formatted: <head n="7." >General Discussion and Theoretical Integration</head>

text.text: The rapid emergence of AI companions has stimulated growing interest in their psychological and relational consequences, giving rise to a rapidly expanding interdisciplinary literature (Döring et al., 2025; Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Smith et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: The central argument of the present article is that understanding these developments requires a conceptual shift in the level of analysis.

AIM conceptualizes Artificial Intimacy as a transformation of the relational ecology within which evolved psychological systems operate, shifting the level of analysis from individual AI companions to the broader relational environment.

This ecological transformation creates novel relational environments that systematically alter the informational conditions regulating human intimacy (Oishi & Graham, 2010; Selçuk et al., 2024; Li et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This ecological transformation creates novel relational environments that systematically alter the informational conditions regulating human intimacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Oishi & Graham, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Selçuk et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Li et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This shift from individual technologies to relational ecology provides the theoretical foundation for integrating diverse psychological phenomena within a single explanatory framework.
This conceptualization represents the principal theoretical contribution of the Artificial Intimacy Model (AIM).

Throughout evolutionary history, human mating and attachment systems evolved within relational environments characterized by interaction with autonomous partners whose availability, responsiveness, and investment were constrained by their own goals, preferences, and competing demands (Bowlby, 1969 (Bowlby, /1982;; Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Finkel et al., 2017; Reis & Clark, 2013).

text.text: AIM argues that Artificial Intimacy does not require the proposal of new psychological mechanisms.

text.text: The central contribution of AIM is therefore the recognition that a transformed relational ecology is sufficient to alter the operation of evolutionarily ancient psychological systems without requiring the proposal of a new psychological mechanism.

This integrative perspective provides a common explanatory framework for organizing existing evidence while generating principled predictions about how future developments in AI-mediated intimacy are likely to influence human relational behavior.

One of the central claims of AIM is that evolutionary psychology provides the most appropriate explanatory framework because it explains why evolutionarily ancient psychological systems respond systematically to the transformed relational ecology created by Artificial Intimacy.

AI-mediated relationships are relevant from an evolutionary perspective because they engage psychological systems that evolved under fundamentally different relational conditions (Buss, 2023; Li et al., 2018; Walter et al., 2020).

text.text: Unlike theoretical approaches that primarily describe the characteristics of AI systems or the experiences of their users (Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026), an evolutionary perspective explains why particular configurations of relational cues are expected to produce predictable psychological responses (Kenrick et al., 2003; Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Within this framework, attachment, mate choice, sexual motivation, jealousy, pair bonding, and relationship maintenance are understood as functionally specialized information-processing systems calibrated to recurrent socioecological conditions rather than to specific technologies or historical contexts (Bowlby, 1969 (Bowlby, /1982;; Buss, 2023; Finkel et al., 2017; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Consequently, the critical scientific question concerns how evolutionarily ancient psychological systems respond when exposed to novel configurations of evolutionarily familiar relational cues.

text.text: This environmental perspective also clarifies the relationship between AIM and several adjacent theoretical traditions.

Attachment theory explains how emotional bonds are formed and maintained (Bowlby, 1969 (Bowlby, /1982;; Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007); parasocial interaction research demonstrates that meaningful relationships can emerge despite structural asymmetry (Hartmann & Goldhoorn, 2011; Horton & Wohl, 1956); and research on anthropomorphism and social presence identifies the perceptual and cognitive processes that facilitate engagement with artificial agents (Epley et al., 2007; Kirk et al., 2025).

text.text: AIM situates these explanations within a broader functional framework by explaining why these apparently distinct psychological phenomena emerge as coordinated responses to the same transformation in relational ecology.
In this respect, AIM complements existing theories by providing a higher-level account of the environmental conditions under which their respective mechanisms are jointly engaged.
This distinction has important implications for future theory development.

As AI technologies continue to evolve, individual platforms, interaction modalities, and forms of artificial companionship will inevitably change (Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Smith et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: Frameworks that are tied primarily to particular technologies or interaction modalities may therefore require continual revision as those technologies evolve.

By contrast, conceptualizing Artificial Intimacy as a transformation of relational ecology shifts the explanatory focus from technological features to the environmental conditions under which evolved psychological systems operate (Li et al., 2018; Oishi & Graham, 2010; Selçuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Several scope conditions deserve particular emphasis.
First, AIM does not predict a single developmental trajectory for Artificial Intimacy or assume that AI companions will inevitably replace human relationships (Malfacini, 2025; Smith et al., 2025).

Artificial Intimacy represents one of the most profound transformations of the human relational landscape since the emergence of digital communication.

As AI companions become increasingly capable of providing emotionally meaningful, personalized, and continuously available interactions, understanding the psychological consequences of this transformed relational ecology will become an increasingly important task for relationship science, evolutionary psychology, and the broader behavioral sciences (Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Smith et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

By conceptualizing Artificial Intimacy as a transformed relational environment rather than merely a technological innovation, AIM provides an integrative explanatory framework linking changes in relational ecology to evolved psychological mechanisms, their behavioral consequences, and a program of empirically testable propositions.

The model complements existing theories of human-AI interaction by offering a higher-level explanatory framework capable of integrating diverse psychological phenomena within a common evolutionary architecture.
Whether Artificial Intimacy ultimately supplements, reshapes, or partially replaces aspects of human relationships remains an empirical question.

What appears increasingly clear, however, is that the relational environments within which human intimacy develops are changing more rapidly than at any previous point in human history (Ho et al., 2025; Malfacini, 2025; Smith et al., 2025; Szczuka et al., 2026).

text.text: Understanding how evolutionarily ancient psychological systems respond to these transformations will therefore be essential for explaining contemporary human relationships and anticipating how the ecology of human intimacy may continue to evolve in an increasingly artificial world.
The significance of Artificial Intimacy may ultimately lie in its capacity to transform the relational ecology within which human nature is expressed.
